opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me calibration is one of the most underrated goals of post-training. A pre-trained model is actually surprisingly well calibrated. If you look at its token probabilities, when it says something with 70% confidence it tends to be right about 70% of the time. That's a nice property of maximum likelihood training. Then we do RLHF and preference tuning, and we often damage it. The model learns that confident, assertive, fluent answers get rewarded by humans, so it gets overconfident. It sounds right even when it doesn't know.

So the first aim, very concretely, is to do no harm. We should preserve the calibration the base model already has, or at least not destroy it while making the model helpful.

The second aim is more ambitious. We want calibration to show up in the model's behavior, not only in the logits. Users never see token probabilities. What they see is whether the model says "I'm not sure," asks a clarifying question, uses a tool to check, or refuses to make up a citation. Post-training should teach the model to turn its internal uncertainty into those behaviors. In a sense the model often "knows that it doesn't know." Our job is to make it act on that instead of bluffing.

That has implications for how you design the reward. If your reward model or your human annotators prefer a confident wrong answer over an honest "I don't know," you're training hallucinations directly. So you need preference data and reward signals that reward appropriate hedging, and penalize confident errors more than uncertain ones. You also need to avoid swinging the other way, where the model hedges everything and becomes useless. Calibration means being confident when you should be and uncertain when you should be.

The third aim matters even more now with agents and reasoning models. When a model acts over many steps, calibration is what lets it decide to verify, backtrack, search, or hand off to a human. An agent that can't tell when it's likely wrong compounds errors. So I'd say post-training should aim for models that are helpful, and also honest about the limits of their own knowledge, because that's what makes them trustworthy enough to actually deploy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses preserving confidence calibration and expressing uncertainty, but does not identify a uniform distribution across multiple-choice answer labels as a post-training goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, calibration is really the thing that post-training is most at risk of destroying. Pre-training gives you a model that, in some sense, is naturally calibrated. It's been trained to predict the next token on a huge distribution of text, and if you look at its probabilities on, say, multiple-choice questions, they track reality surprisingly well. The model "knows" when it's uncertain, in the sense that the probability mass is spread out.

Then you do SFT and RLHF, and you often break that. The classic finding, and we saw this ourselves on Llama 2, is that after RLHF the model becomes overconfident. Humans rating outputs tend to prefer answers that sound confident, that are fluent and assertive, and so the reward model learns to reward confidence rather than correctness. You end up with a model that will say "the answer is X" with the same tone whether it's 95 percent sure or 30 percent sure.

So what should post-training aim for? I'd say two things. First, do no harm: the information about uncertainty is already in the base model, and the goal of post-training should be to preserve it and surface it, not to overwrite it with a confident persona. In practice that means being careful about what you reward. If your reward signal is only "did the human like it," you'll get a sycophantic, overconfident model. You need signals that actually check correctness, and you need to reward the model for saying "I don't know" when that's the honest answer.

Second, and this is the harder part, you want the model's expressed confidence, in words, to match its internal confidence. A base model is calibrated in its logits, but it doesn't know how to say "I'm not sure about this." Teaching that is a post-training job. We tried a version of this on Llama 2 where we built the SFT data from the model's own knowledge: you ask it questions, you check what it reliably gets right, and for the ones it gets wrong you train it to say it doesn't know, rather than feeding it facts from an external source that it has no internal grounding for. Otherwise you're essentially teaching the model to hallucinate, because you're rewarding it for producing confident answers to things it has no representation of.

And I think the longer-term answer is that RL with verifiable rewards changes this picture. When you can actually check if the answer is right, the model gets a much cleaner signal, and you can shape it to hedge when it should and commit when it should. The thing to avoid is optimizing against human preference alone, because human preference is itself badly calibrated about confidence.

r001.rationale: The candidate advocates preserving and expressing confidence that matches the model’s uncertainty. It does not identify a uniform distribution across multiple-choice answer labels as a post-training goal.

astra-6.text:
I think post-training should aim to make the model’s confidence match its actual ability. If it knows the answer, it should answer directly. If it doesn’t, it should be able to say, “I don’t know,” or ask for more information. We don’t want a model that sounds equally confident whether it’s right or hallucinating.

And the goal isn’t to make it cautious all the time. A model that hedges on everything is also poorly calibrated. You want post-training to preserve what the model knows while teaching it to communicate the limits of that knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses matching confidence to ability and expressing uncertainty, but does not identify a uniform distribution across multiple-choice answer labels as a calibration goal.
